case_name: D.M. v Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director)
text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation:
D.M. v Alberta (
Child, Youth and
Family Enhancement Act
,
Director)
, 2017 ABPC 12

Date:
20170124

Docket:
FF901003796

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

D.M.

Applicant

- and -

Director of Child and Family Services

Respondent

Restriction on Publication

Identification Ban
– See the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act
,

section
126.2
.

No one may publish the name or
photograph of a child, or of the child's parent or guardian, in a way that
reveals that the child is receiving, or has received, intervention services.

NOTE:

This judgment is intended to comply with the restriction so that it may be
published.

Reasons for Decision of the
Honourable

R.J. O'Gorman

Assistant Chief Judge

Current Application

[
1
]

On December 7, 2016, the paternal grandfather,
D.M., filed a Family Law claim under the
Family Law Act
[1]
seeking to terminate guardianship over his three grandchildren.
Currently, the Director of Child and Family Services (“the Director”) has
guardianship of the three children pursuant to an Order of Permanent
Guardianship (“PGO”) granted by the Honorable Judge J. Shaw on October 22,
2014. As Assistant Chief Judge, I directed that the grandfather would require
Leave of the Court in order for him to proceed any further with his application
and that hearing was scheduled in front of me on January 12, 2017.

[
2
]

Therefore, this is in regards to the hearing for
the Leave application by the grandfather. The paternal grandparents, as well as
the paternal uncle, had previously applied for guardianship of the three
children. All three applications were dismissed by Judge Shaw on October 22,
2014, when he granted PGO to the Director.

[
3
]

The paternal grandparents and the paternal uncle
appealed the decision to the Court of Queen’s Bench. On November 25, 2015, the
Honorable Justice C. Dario dismissed their appeals. A further application was
made to Justice Dario to reinstate the appeals, which was denied on August 18,
2016. A final appeal was made to the Honorable Justice B. MacDonald of the
Alberta Court of Appeal to reinstate the appeals, which was denied on December
13, 2016.

Is there a Cause of Action?

[
4
]

The first issue that arises is whether the
grandfather has a recognized cause of action that would permit him to pursue a
claim under the
Family Law Act
.
[2]
Although the grandfather
wrote in his claim that he was applying to terminate the children’s
guardianship, at the Leave application on January 12, 2017, he stated he was
actually applying “for guardianship” of his grandchildren. The grandfather’s
previous application for guardianship was clearly dismissed by Judge Shaw on
October 22, 2014. The doctrine of
res judicata
will be discussed
shortly. In any event, the essence of the grandfather’s claim is that they have
rights because they were the children’s “
de facto
parents” and in “
loco
parentis
”. This claim that they have acquired rights has been repeatedly
rejected by the courts and specifically by Justice Dario at page 14 and 15 of
her August 18, 2016 decision. In fact, at page 15, line 19, Justice Dario
states that the whole point of the trial in front of Judge Shaw was whether the
grandparents should be named guardians (which they were not).

[
5
]

The applicable section of the
Family Law Act

regarding termination of guardianship is
s. 25(1)
, which states:

Termination of guardianship

25(1) The court may, on application by a
guardian or a proposed guardian, make an order terminating the guardianship of
a guardian, including the applicant, if there is a guardian in place or about
to be appointed and if

(a) the court is satisfied that the guardian
whose guardianship is to be terminated consents to the termination, or

(b) for reasons that appear to it to be
sufficient, the court considers it necessary or desirable to do so.

[
6
]

The children are not subject to guardianship
under the
Family Law Act
[3]
. The Director is the permanent guardian of the children under the
Child,
Youth and Family Enhancement Act
[4]
. Pursuant to
s. 34

of the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act
[5]
, a PGO to the Director was granted for all three children. The paternal
grandparents have previously applied for access to the children in accordance
with s. 34(8) of the
Act
and have been repeatedly turned down.
Therefore, it is simply not possible for the grandfather to apply under the
Family
Law Act
to try and terminate the PGO of the Director. There is simply no
cause of action available to the grandfather. Even if there is a possible cause
of action, there are other significant problems with the grandfather’s
application.

Is the Doctrine of
Res Judicata
Applicable Here?

[
7
]

The doctrine of
res judicata
is a rule
that a final judgement on the merits by a Court having jurisdiction is
conclusive between the parties as to all matters that were litigated in that
case or could have been litigated in that case.
[6]
The doctrine
is to prevent re-litigation of something that has been previously decided,
ensuring finality in litigation.
[7]

Public policy “...has
dictated that once the right of appeal has been exhausted, judicial decisions
should be conclusive”.
[8]

[
8
]

The doctrine of
res judicata
has developed
to maintain respect for the administration of justice.
[9]

It is a cornerstone of our legal system. The system depends on finality, the
guiding principle being “
interest rei publicae at finis sit litium
”, or “It
is in the interest of the public that litigation come to an end”.
[10]

[
9
]

Issue estoppel
is
a branch of
res jidicata,
which precludes the re-litigation of issues
previously decided in court in another proceeding.
[11]

The three elements of
issue estoppel
are set out by the Supreme Court of
Canada as follows:

1.

That the same question has been decided;

2.

That the judicial decision which is said to
create the estoppel was final; and

3.

That the parties to the judicial decision or
their privies were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which
the estoppel is raised.
[12]

[
10
]

At the Leave hearing, the grandfather had
attempted to argue that the merits of his appeal had never been properly heard.
Once again, I cannot agree with the grandfather. Although it was technically an
application to reinstate their appeal in the Court of Queen’s Bench, the
reality is that the proceedings in front of Justice Dario represented a
thorough review of each and every ground of appeal the grandparents had listed.
Any procedural difficulties or legal irregularities that have arisen with the
appeals are almost entirely the fault of the grandparents. The fact that both
grandparents declined to testify at the 20-day trial in front of Judge Shaw is
very perplexing. In addition, some of the grandparents’ arguments have been
nonsensical, inflammatory and defamatory.

[
11
]

Prior to further reviewing the decision of
Justice Dario, it may be helpful to explain how the appeal was originally
struck. Whether done inadvertently or with deliberate intent, the grandparents
failed to order transcripts for every day of trial that had occurred in front
of Judge Shaw. It turned out that from the 20 days of the trial, two days of
transcripts were not ordered by the grandparents.
[13]

The
Alberta Rules of Court
[14]
,
Rule 12.65(1)
,
states:

If the appellant does not comply with rule
12.63(2), the Court must order that the appeal be dismissed, with or without
costs, without further notice to the appellant.

[
12
]

Rule 12.63(2) states that within three months of
filing the notice of appeal, the appellant must file a copy of the transcript
with the Court of Queen’s Bench and serve a copy on the respondent. There is a
discretionary provision contained in rule 12.65(2) stating:

The Court may, on application, reinstate an
appeal that has been dismissed under this rule.

[
13
]

In front of Justice Dario, the grandparents
initially argued that they had requested the transcripts for all of the trial
days and that the Transcript Management Services had made a mistake. In fact,
as Assistant Chief Judge, I had written a letter on December 17, 2015,
confirming that the two days of missing transcripts were not part of the
original order from the grandparents. The grandparents next accused Judge Shaw
of somehow intentionally withholding those two days of transcripts. This
allegation is simply absurd. Next, the grandparents argued that the Court Order
of the Honorable Justice P. Sullivan, granted on November 12, 2014, had only
stated that they “pay” for the full transcript and not that they actually
order, file and serve a full transcript. Justice Dario shows immense patience
with the grandparents when she states that they have unreasonably interpreted Justice
Sullivan’s Court Order. In fact, Justice Dario reads the exact wording from
Justice Sullivan’s Order, which reads:

The Appellants shall request from Transcript
Management and shall pay for a full transcript of proceedings of the trial of
the matter, and shall file and serve the transcript on the respondent on or
before January 27, 2015.

[
14
]

Justice Dario notes that the grandparents had
not, in fact, paid for the full transcript, as they had not ordered a full
transcript. Finally, the grandparents had argued that as self-represented
litigants, they had just made a mistake and that the two days of missing
transcripts were insignificant. Justice Dario specifically reviewed the 121
pages of the missing transcripts. Contrary to the grandparents’ position,
Justice Dario found the missing testimony to be very relevant evidence to any
appeal.
[15]

[
15
]

With respect to the missing transcripts, Justice
Dario finds the grandparents’ position all very troubling. In any event,
Justice Dario notes that the grandparents have also raised the issues of bias
and conspiracy against both Judge Shaw and the Director. Under the heading
“Arguable Merit to the Appeal”, Justice Dario states at page 10, starting at
line 5:

This brings us to the determination element
of the test in this case, whether there is arguable merit to the applicants’
appeal. This element of the application is an assessment of whether the applicants
would have any probability of success in their appeal. It is not a procedural
issue but a substantive analysis. If the reinstatement application is
unsuccessful, it will result in a dismissal of the appeal. Given the possible
outcome, I have gone through this element of the application in a great amount
of detail. Specifically, I have read every page of the over 2,000 pages of
trial transcripts, as well as affidavits and the submissions of the parties in
this application, in addition to hearing oral submissions on February 1, 2016,
and reviewed certain other evidence or exhibits to the trial.

I am confirming the extent of the review I
have undertaken to ensure that there is no suggestion that I have made this
determination based on a mere technicality. Instead, I have made a substantive
review of all of the applicants’ arguments, both written submissions filed for
the appeal and oral submissions made in this application, after a full review
of the trial transcript, in order to determine if the applicants have met this
element of the test for reinstatement.

The test to establish merit to this appeal
requires that the grandparents have a reasonable prospect of success or at the
very least an arguable case. It cannot be a baseless appeal.

Is there any Arguable Merit to the Appeal?

[
16
]

Justice Dario reviews
the case law dealing with arguable merit and that it is, in fact, a low
threshold. Justice Dario states that in assessing whether there is a reasonable
basis to appeal, it is important for the parties to note that an appeal is not
merely a second opportunity to have the matter reheard or re-decided. The
appellate court must find a basis for the appeal, such as that the trial judge
erred in law or in fact to a degree that would merit an appellate court intervention.
With this in mind, Justice Dario summarized the grandparents’ grounds for their
appeal as follows:

1.

Bias of the trial judge;

2.

Failure by the trial judge to apply the correct
legal test;

3.

Errors in fact-finding by the trial judge;

4.

Fresh evidence;

5.

Charter
[16]
violations; and

6.

Conspiracy of the judge, Director and others
involved.

[
17
]

With respect to the allegation of bias against
Judge Shaw, Justice Dario conducted an extensive review of the trial and
concluded, “I find that the trial judge was not biased; rather, he was
deferential and demonstrated a conscientious attempt to ensure fairness to the
applicants”.
[17]
With regard to the
allegation that the trial judge failed to apply the correct legal test, Justice
Dario stated that the trial judge was well aware of the order of events, as
required by the legislation and case law, and that this was confirmed during
the trial and the judge’s decision.

[
18
]

Next, the grandparents had alleged that the
trial judge made errors in his finding of fact. Justice Dario noted that
neither grandparent testified at the trial and that the trial judge was
entitled to draw an adverse inference from this fact. Justice Dario stated that
the “...overwhelming majority of the evidence supported the trial judge’s
decision, not specifically to credibility, but on the whole of his decision”.
[18]

Justice Dario noted that the grandparents had alleged a number of other
factual errors by the trial judge. In fact, the grandparents had alleged that
somehow Judge Shaw had either ignored or potentially participated in the
cover-up of medical evidence that could have identified the actual perpetrator
of the sexual assault. The grandparents suggested that Judge Shaw ignored
evidence tampering because a dirty diaper had not been retained for testing
after the children had returned from a visit to Saskatchewan where they stayed
with the maternal grandparents. Justice Dario noted that the evidence at trial
was that the children’s father had repeatedly failed to take the children for a
medical examination as requested and that the children had repeatedly disclosed
that their father was the sexual perpetrator.
[19]

[
19
]

The grandparents also raised fresh evidence as
an example that the trial judge has misapprehended the facts. Specifically, the
grandparents pointed to a recent conviction against the maternal grandfather
for sexual assault upon one of his daughters, a sister to the children’s
mother. Justice Dario determined that the existence of a conviction against the
maternal grandfather does not prove that the trial judge’s decision should be
interfered with. In fact, Justice Dario notes that since being removed from
their parents’ care, the older children have repeatedly identified their father
as the sexual perpetrator and have denied any wrongdoing by the maternal
grandfather. Justice Dario also noted that there was evidence that the paternal
grandparents had attempted to convince the children to recant their statements
that their father was the sexual perpetrator.
[20]

[
20
]

Next, the grandparents had alleged a number of
Charter

violations. The grandparents have suggested violations of s. 7, 10 and 11 of
the
Charter
.
[21]
Justice Dario summarises
the grandparents’ position as being that the children should have been placed
with the paternal grandparents. The grandparents had also argued that the
children’s rights were violated because the Director had “unlawfully
incarcerated” the children into the Director’s care. Justice Dario noted that
the whole point of Child and Family Services intervention is to ensure the
children’s safety. Justice Dario also noted that the grandparents believe that
the children should not have been apprehended without hard medical evidence.
Justice Dario questions how much more medical evidence is necessary than
medical evidence that a young girl’s hymen had been severed before the Director
should intervene to protect the children.

[
21
]

Somehow related to the grandparents’ allegations
of
Charter
violations is their claim of anti-Semitism. The grandparents
have accused the Director of anti-Semitism. Surprisingly, the grandparents have
also accused the Calgary Jewish Academy of being anti-Semitic. Justice Dario
stated that the grandparents appeared to be putting their own interests ahead
of the grandchildren. Justice Dario also stated that this was consistent with
the findings of Judge Shaw. Justice Dario finally noted that the grandparents
had requested that the Director deny any visitation to the children by any
relatives of Gentile heritage. Justice Dario states that this is a clear
example of the grandparents’ double standard and is a completely inappropriate
request. I unequivocally concur.

[
22
]

The final basis of appeal raised by the
grandparents is that there has been a conspiracy against them. The grandparents
have alleged that essentially everyone who does not support them is against
them. This list included the Director, the Judge, caseworkers, psychologists,
therapists, the Calgary Jewish Centre, the Jewish Academy, the medical
professionals and the foster parents. Judge Dario found the grandparents’
allegations to be “unfounded, unsubstantiated allegations that are offensive to
this court”.
[22]
Justice Dario stated,
“To say that this basis of appeal is farfetched would be an understatement. I
found no reasonable basis for the appeal on this ground.”
[23]

Application to Reinstate Appeal Denied

[
23
]

In her conclusion, Justice Dario denies the
application by the paternal grandparents to reinstate their appeal. Justice
Dario stated at page 27, starting at line 10, of the August 18, 2016
Transcript, the following:

In conclusion, I find that none of the
arguments raised by the applicants suggests a reasonable basis for appeal, and
I therefore decline to reinstate the appeal.

At the end of all of these statements, I do
not think that there is a legal argument or lists of facts that I could refer
to that would satisfy the applicants in this case. The only satisfactory result
to the applicants would be the return of the grandchildren to their care and a
declaration of the (father’s) innocence of all allegations. The Court cannot do
that, however. It is the (grandparents) unwillingness to consider the
possibility that their son could have been the abuser against the children
which was and continues to be the material factor in the decision not to grant
guardianship to the applicants. This refusal to consider that harm may come to
the children by ignoring the numerous disclosures made voluntarily by the
children to police officers, Child and Family Service workers, and foster
parents essentially prohibits the Court from granting guardianship of the
children to the applicants. The protection of the children from physical and
emotional trauma or abuse is the basis for granting the Director permanent
guardianship over the children.

Is the Grandfather a Vexatious Litigant?

[
24
]

At this stage, it becomes necessary to consider
whether the paternal grandfather should be found to be a frivolous and
vexatious litigant. It is beyond doubt that the grandfather has engaged in a
deliberate course of conduct that is bizarre and at times nonsensical and
inflammatory. It has been suggested that to attract the designation of being a
“vexatious” litigant the Court should review the character and nature of the
litigant’s actions, including the entire history of the dispute, inside and
outside the courtroom.
[24]
Repeated applications by the same litigant involving the same
children, regarding the same issues where the court has made a clear ruling,
which has been conveyed to the litigant, may give rise to such a finding of
being a vexatious litigant.
[25]
In our case, the grandfather has been clearly advised of the
finality of the litigation. Justice Dario made the following statement to the
grandparents when refusing to reinstate the appeal:

I took a lot of time coming to this decision
and you can tell I looked at everything, but you need to respect the decision
of the court and come to terms with it. You will also need to respect the
position of the Director in declining access at this time to your
grandchildren.
[26]

[
25
]

In
Gauthier v. Starr
,
[27]
Associate Chief Justice J. Rooke reviewed the current cases dealing
with the principles and indicia to identify vexatious litigants. Justice Rooke
referred to Justice D. Shelley’s decision in
Kavanagh v. Kavanagh
,
[28]
where a misuse and abuse of the legal process was highlighted in
such a test to determine a vexatious litigant. Justice Shelley had stated at
para 64:

All misuse of legal procedure in a manner
that has no valid purpose, and, as a consequence, causes harm to involved
litigants and the waste of court resources. While non-legal dictionary
definitions of “vexatious” focus on an act being wrongful, harassing,
malicious, or intended to annoy, the legal meaning of this word is broader. A
vexatious proceeding is one that in effect abuses or misuses legal processes.

[
26
]

Our Alberta Court of Appeal has also emphasised
the connection to abuse. In
420093 B.C. Ltd. v. Bank of Montreal
[29]
Justice W. O’Leary stated:

In my view the present action is manifestly
an abuse of process. It is an attempt to re-litigate issues and causes of
action which have already been decided or are deemed to have been decided. ... It
is time that the litigation came to an end.

[
27
]

The provisions of the
Family Law Act
[30]
that deal with a vexatious litigant are found in
s. 91(1)
, which
states as follows:

Where the court is satisfied
t
hat a person has made a frivolous or vexatious
application to the court, the court may prohibit that person from making
further applications under this Act without the permission of the court.

[
28
]

There is no doubt that the paternal grandfather
is a frivolous and vexatious litigant. His behavior in and outside of the courtroom
is outrageous. In the Provincial Court there have been 54 appearances under the

Family Law Act
[31]
and 57 appearances under the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement
Act
.
[32]
In addition to these
court appearances, there are also the court appearances in the Court of Queen’s
Bench and the Court of Appeal.

[
29
]

The grandparents, as well as the children’s
father, have engaged in numerous defamatory accusations against nearly everyone
who does not support them. These irrational statements have included the
following:

•

Accusing the Calgary Jewish Academy of being
anti-Semitic;

•

Accusing the Jewish Family Services of being
anti-Semitic;

•

Accusing the Director of being anti-Semitic;

•

Calling a Child and Family Services worker a
Muslim terrorist;

•

Comparing Child and Family Services to Nazi
Germany, accusing Child and Family Services of “Jew hatred by an Alberta
Government machinery”;

•

Accusing the Director of brainwashing the
children;

•

Accusing the Director of manufacturing evidence
against the father;

•

Referring to the PGO trial as a “Kangaroo court”;

•

Alleging the children suffer from Stockholm
syndrome; and

•

Alleging the Provincial Court and just about
everyone else is biased against them.

[
30
]

The grandparents have also repeatedly attempted
to discover the location of the children in foster care. A former foster home
placement broke down because the grandparents discovered the location and would
not stay away. The children had to be moved to another foster home. In August
2016, the grandparents contacted the Jewish community suggesting that one of
the children had been killed in a car crash. The grandparents contacted the
police and were told the information was incorrect. The police also told the
grandparents to contact Child and Family Services in the future. The Director
is concerned that the grandparents have now done this twice and that it is
likely a future attempt to try and elicit some information about where the
children are placed could occur.

[
31
]

The grandparents have also published the names
of the grandchildren, stating that the maternal grandfather sexually abused
them. The grandparents have been warned that the publication of the children’s
identities is strictly prohibited under the
Child, Youth and Family
Enhancement Act
.
[33]
There is also a ‘go-fund-me’ website that has identified the
children’s names that is allegedly connected to the grandparents, although the
grandparents deny involvement with it.
[34]

[
32
]

Although I have found the paternal grandfather
to be a vexatious litigant under the
Family Law Act
,
[35]
a vexatious proceedings, or conducting a proceeding in a vexatious
manner, is also set out in
s.
23 of the

Judicature
Act
(as amended)
[36]
.
Section 23(2)
includes, without limitation, any one or more of the
following:

(a)

persistently bringing proceedings to determine
an issue that has already been determined by a court of competent jurisdiction;

(b)

persistently bringing proceedings that cannot
succeed or that have no reasonable expectation of providing relief;

(c)

persistently bringing proceedings for improper
purposes;

(d)

persistently using previously raised grounds and
issues in subsequent proceedings inappropriately;

(e)

persistently failing to pay the costs of
unsuccessful proceedings on the part of the person who commenced those
proceedings;

(f)

persistently taking unsuccessful appeals from
judicial decisions; and

(g)

persistently engaging in inappropriate courtroom
behaviour.

Conclusion

[
33
]

The paternal grandfather’s application to terminate
guardianship or to seek guardianship of his three grandchildren is hereby
dismissed. The paternal grandfather is found to be a frivolous and vexatious
applicant to the Court pursuant to
s. 91(1)
of the
Family Law Ac
t
[37]
. The paternal grandfather is therefore prohibited from making any
further applications under the
Family Law Act
[38]
,
the
Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act
[39]
, or any other legislation in the Province of Alberta or Canada
without the permission of the Court. Finally, the paternal grandfather shall
pay costs to the Director of Child and Family Services in the amount of
$5,000.00, payable to the Clerk of Court forthwith.

Heard on the
12
th
day of January, 2017.

Dated at the
City of Calgary, Alberta this 24
th
day of
January, 2017.

R.J. O'Gorman

A Judge of the
Provincial Court of Alberta

treating children who had been abused, and she had testified to handwritten
drawings the child had made depicting the sexual assaults and the identity of
the alleged perpetrator.

[16]

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Being Part 1 of the

Constitution Act
, 1982.

Transcript of August 18, 2016, page 12, line 32. In addition,
Justice Dario attached an Appendix “A” to the transcript containing 27 examples
where the trial judge intervened on a number of occasions to primarily protect
the grandparents’ position and to explain the trial process to the
grandparents.

[18]
Transcript of August 18, 2016, page 17, line 36

father, the oldest child had, on video, accused the maternal grandfather of abuse,
but since then, the child has only accused the father.

[20]

the challenge and strain an inter-familial sexual abuse allegation can place on
family members. Some family members may find it hard to accept that the abuser
could do such a thing. The same therapist also testified to the potential
negative impact on the children if they feel they are not believed or
supported. These could range from depression, anxiety, sleep disturbances, poor
emotional regulation, post-traumatic stress symptoms and an impaired sense of
self.
